{ "d_study_links": "", "d_avma_study_data": { "patients_randomly_assigned": true, "investigator_aware": true, "owners_aware": true, "vct_code": "VCT26005993", "selection_species": "", "selection_study_type": "", "selection_control_group_therapy": "", "selection_intervention_type": "", "selection_financial_incentive": "", "selection_primary_field": "" }, "d_avma_studycontent_data": { "potential_benefits": "

Benefits are unknown but the hope is for improved neurological symptoms, tumor shrinkage and improved quality of life.


Your pet may not get any benefit from being in this research study. This treatment has a sound medical basis but is the subject of this clinical trial because it has not been used in animals in the same way as it is being tested in this study. Your pet’s disease may get better, stay the same, or get worse while participating in this study.

", "potential_risks": "

Risks associated with blood draws

The risk of blood draws and catheter placement include discomfort, mild redness, bruising, and very rarely infection at the site of blood sampling. In some cases, it is necessary to clip the hair over the vein in order to facilitate collection of a blood sample.


Risks of general anesthesia

Anesthetic drugs often affect blood pressure, heart rate, breathing, and body temperature; we monitor vital signs continuously during and after anesthesia. Complications can happen, but life-threatening ones are uncommon. The complications include decreased heart rate and blood pressure, poor oxygenation and tissue perfusion (cyanosis), trauma to the respiratory tract due to intubation, aspiration pneumonia, gastrointestinal upset (such as vomiting and diarrhea), catheter site inflammation and infection, acute kidney injury, allergy to anesthetic drugs, cardiopulmonary arrest, and death. You can ask to discuss the risks with your care provider team prior to the anesthetic event, and you will be asked to sign the hospital’s standard consent form for general anesthesia during the visit.


Risks of radiation therapy for brain tumors

Radiation therapy is commonly used to treat brain tumors in dogs and is generally well tolerated. However, side effects can occur. Some side effects happen during or shortly after treatment, while others may develop weeks to months later. Because FLASH proton radiation therapy is still being studied, there may also be risks or side effects that are not yet known.


Acute Side Effects (during treatment to approximately 3 months after treatment): These side effects are usually temporary and can often be managed with medications. Rarely, they can be unresponsive to medical management and life-threatening.

Signs may include:

  1. Tiredness or decreased activity
  2. Reduced appetite or nausea
  3. Temporary swelling of the brain because of inflammation and edema, which may cause worsening of neurologic signs such as seizures, weakness, imbalance, behavior changes, or decreased alertness.
  4. In rare cases, severe brain swelling requires hospitalization or intensive care.


Delayed Acute Side Effects (weeks to a few months after treatment): Some dogs experience temporary worsening of neurologic signs after an initial period of improvement.

Signs may include:

  1. New or worsening seizures
  2. Weakness or difficulty walking
  3. Changes in behavior
  4. Reduced alertness or confusion


These changes are often treated with medications such as corticosteroids and may improve over time.


Late Side Effects (more than 3 months after treatment, usually months to years after): Late side effects are less common but may be permanent.

Signs may include:

  1. Persistent or new neurologic problems, including seizures, weakness, balance problems, vision changes, or behavior changes.
  2. Damage to normal brain tissue (radiation necrosis) or stroke-like injury, which may cause symptoms similar to those caused by the tumor.
  3. Although uncommon, severe radiation-related complications can significantly affect quality of life and, in rare cases, may be life-threatening.


Your dog will be monitored closely throughout the study with physical examinations, neurologic evaluations, and MRI scans.

If significant side effects occur, appropriate treatment will be provided, and your dog may be withdrawn from the study if continued participation is no longer in their best interest.


Potential risks associated with Gilvetmab

Gilvetmab is a specific antibody, a special protein made by the immune system, to find and destroy germs like bacteria and viruses, that aims to enhance a dog’s ability for its’ own immune system to attack cancer cells.

In healthy and cancer-bearing dogs who had previously received Gilvetmab, negative side-effects were mostly mild, resolved with treatment, and occurred in less than 40% of patients.


The negative side effects include lethargy/fatigue, reduced appetite, vomiting, weight loss, increased liver enzymes (ALP, ALT, AST), anemia (low red blood cells), nausea, proteinuria (increased protein in the urine), tumor hemorrhage (bleeding) or hypotension (low blood pressure, but only in dogs with mast cell tumor), hypersensitivity/allergic reaction, anaphylaxis, muscle weakness, tremor. Based on human medicine experience, autoimmune disease can occur with ICIs; examples are listed below, but clinically, these immune-related diseases have not been reported in the previous canine clinical trial.


There is a possibility that your dog’s immune cells could not only attack your dog’s cancer cells but also other cells in your dog’s body. This condition, in which immune cells begin to attack your own tissues, is known as “autoimmune disease.” Autoimmune disease can affect many parts of the body, such as the skin, kidneys, nerves, muscles, the endocrine system (the system that directs the body’s hormones and other chemicals), and the digestive system (gut). If your dog develops an autoimmune disease, he/she will need to be treated with corticosteroids alone or in combination with other immunosuppressive drugs to try to prevent immune cells from damaging healthy tissues. If your dog were to develop an autoimmune disease, they may be removed from the study on a case-by-case basis.


Please note: There may also be unknown risks that are not yet identified. If your pet becomes ill, you should inform any veterinarian that your pet is participating in a research study.


Risks of obtaining tumor biopsies in the brain (optional)

A brain tumor biopsy involves removing a small sample of the tumor using a needle-like or surgical instrument while your dog is under general anesthesia. Although this procedure is commonly performed by experienced veterinary specialists, it carries risks because the brain is a sensitive organ.


Possible risks include:

\n- Bleeding within or around the brain, which may cause neurologic problems and, in rare cases, require emergency treatment.

\n- Swelling of the brain, which can temporarily or permanently worsen neurologic signs.

\n- Infection, although this is uncommon because the procedure is performed using sterile techniques.

\n- Temporary or permanent neurologic changes, such as weakness, difficulty walking, vision changes, changes in behavior, or seizures, depending on the location of the tumor.

\n- Failure to obtain a diagnostic sample, meaning the biopsy may not provide enough tissue to make a diagnosis or complete all planned research tests.

\n- Death, although extremely uncommon, is a potential risk of any invasive brain procedure.

Your dog's imaging studies will be carefully reviewed before the biopsy, and the procedure will only be performed by experienced veterinary neurosurgeons. If, at the time of the procedure, the biopsy is considered unsafe, it will not be performed.

Risks of collecting cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)

CSF collection is a commonly performed procedure in veterinary neurology and is generally considered safe when performed by experienced clinicians. However, as with any medical procedure, there are some risks. Possible risks include:

\n- Mild pain or soreness at the collection site after the procedure

\n- Temporary worsening of neurologic signs, such as weakness, imbalance, or seizures

\n- Bleeding at the collection site or, rarely, around the brain or spinal cord

\n- Infection, although this is uncommon because sterile techniques are used

\n- Temporary leakage of spinal fluid, which usually resolves on its own

\n- In very rare cases, severe neurologic complications, including brain herniation (movement of brain tissue due to increased pressure inside the skull), paralysis, coma, or death


Before collecting CSF, your dog will undergo brain imaging (MRI) to help determine whether the procedure can be performed safely. If the procedure is considered unsafe, it will not be performed.


Risks of Urine Collection

We will collect a urine sample whenever possible using a free-catch method, which means collecting urine while your dog urinates naturally. There are no known risks associated with collecting a free-catch urine sample. If a free-catch sample cannot be obtained, or is not suitable for testing, we may recommend cystocentesis. Cystocentesis is a standard veterinary procedure involving the sterile collection of a urine sample by inserting a needle into the urinary bladder through the abdominal wall. Risks of this procedure can include: discomfort, mild redness, bruising or bleeding, leaking of urine in the abdomen, and, very rarely, infection at the site of urine collection.

", "sec_outcome1_name": "", "sec_outcome1_measure": "", "sec_outcome1_endpoint": "", "sec_outcome2_name": "", "sec_outcome2_measure": "", "sec_outcome2_endpoint": "", "study_results": "", "funding_source_names": "", "funding_source_government": false, "funding_source_foundation": false, "funding_source_company": false, "funding_source_institution": true, "funding_source_none": false }, "d_sv_content": { "id": "30501", "name": "FLASH-Based Radioimmunotherapy in Canine Glioma", "tagline": "FLASH RT in Canine Glioma", "speciesListDisplay": "", "ageRange": "", "studyType": "", "description": "

The purpose of this study is to evaluate the feasibility, safety, and efficacy of FLASH proton radiation therapy (FLASH-RT), administered either alone or in combination with Gilvetmab, as a treatment for canine brain tumors (gliomas), with the goal of providing effective tumor control while reducing treatment-related side effects. FLASH-RT, combined with Gilvetmab, is considered experimental.


This trial offers three doses of FLASH-RT targeted for canine glioma with randomization to also receive three infusions of Gilvetmab following the RT protocol.


The three radiation therapy treatments happen on separate visits - usually Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. They are performed using standard of care general anesthesia. 


FLASH-RT: FLASH-RT treatments are performed at the Smilow Translational Research Building (STRB) in the evenings. This is a separate building a few blocks away from the veterinary hospital. Your dog will be transported to this building along with the study personnel, usually between 5-8 PM. Your dog will be anesthetized for the FLASH-RT treatments. Once your dog is recovered from anesthesia, he or she will be transported back to Penn Vet Ryan Hospital, usually between 10-12 PM. Your dog can go home that night or the following morning if recovery is slower than expected or if additional monitoring or supportive care is needed.

", "sec_outcome2_name": "", "sec_outcome2_measure": "", "sec_outcome2_endpoint": "", "study_results": "", "funding_source_names": "", "funding_source_government": null, "funding_source_foundation": null, "funding_source_company": null, "funding_source_institution": null, "funding_source_none": true }, "d_sv_content": { "id": "29175", "name": "Combination chemotherapy (Doxorubicin-Temozolomide with or without propranolol) in dogs with Hemangiosarcoma", "tagline": "Evaluation of combination chemotherapy for hemangiosarcoma", "speciesListDisplay": "", "ageRange": "", "studyType": "", "description": "

The objective of this study is to investigate the effectiveness of combining doxorubicin and temozolomide with or without propranolol in dogs with hemangiosarcoma. The use of either doxorubicin alone as a treatment for hemangiosarcoma has been studied, and studies with propranolol (historically used to treat heart disease) have shown promise as an added treatment against hemangiosarcoma, however, survival times still remain quite low. A sister drug to Temozolomide, DTIC, has shown promise in improving survival times, however side effects and the long administration times have created challenges with the use of DTIC in dogs. Temozolomide is administered orally and is historically well tolerated in dogs. We are hopeful that survival times can be further improved using a combination approach to treatment, with combination of both intravenous and oral treatments and improved tolerability. Dogs with hemangiosarcoma of the spleen, liver, heart or intramuscular region will be considered for inclusion in this study.

", "sec_outcome2_name": "", "sec_outcome2_measure": "", "sec_outcome2_endpoint": "", "study_results": "", "funding_source_names": "", "funding_source_government": null, "funding_source_foundation": null, "funding_source_company": null, "funding_source_institution": true, "funding_source_none": null }, "d_sv_content": { "id": "29459", "name": "Novel Immunotherapy for Cats with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma", "tagline": "New Treatment for Cats with Oral Tumors", "speciesListDisplay": "", "ageRange": "", "studyType": "", "description": "

Oral squamous cell carcinoma is a very difficult cancer to treat in cats and is often fairly advanced before it is detected. This clinical trial will be examining the effectiveness of a new type of immunotherapy for treating this disease in cats, which is based on very promising data from two squamous cell carcinoma trials conducted recently in horses at CSU. This new treatment is designed to stimulate the body’s own immune defenses to attack the tumor cells and cause tumor regression or elimination. In this particular trial, even stopping the tumor from growing (rather than full elimination) would be considered a success. This immunotherapy drug has been tested previously in cats, and is generally well-tolerated, with few side-effects, but it has only been evaluated in one cat with oral squamous cell carcinoma previously. The treatment has however been extensively evaluated in horses with squamous cell carcinoma, with a high degree of success. In this study, we will evaluate this novel immunotherapy in cats with oral SCC to determine how well the treatment works and how well it is tolerated by cats.


Cats will receive four injections of the LTN immunotherapy into their tumor, which are given once every three weeks. Cats must be put under anesthesia for these injections. While under anesthesia, cats will have CT scans and tumor biopsies performed prior to starting treatment, at the time of the third injection, and 3 weeks after the 4th injection (CT only). Blood tests (complete blood count and chemistry profile) will also be performed at these visits. Study participation is completed after the visit that is 3 weeks after the last injection. A total of 5 visits and anesthetic episodes are required for this study.

Electrochemotherapy is a valuable anti-cancer therapy in both human and veterinary patients. Until recently, there was no electrode to allow treatment of bone lesions. Veterinary Oncology Services (www.petcancerinformation.com) has a bone electrode used in human applications (see below).


Curr Oncol. 2022 Mar 4;29(3):1672-1682. doi: 10.3390/curroncol29030139.

Electrochemotherapy Is Effective in the Treatment of Bone Metastases

Laura Campanacci 1, Luca Cevolani 1, Francesca De Terlizzi 2, Laura Saenz 3, Nikolin Alì 1, Giuseppe Bianchi 1, Davide Maria Donati 1


Abstract

Bone metastases induce pain, risk of fracture, and neural compression, and reduced mobility and quality of life. Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a minimally invasive local treatment based on a high-voltage electric pulse combined with an anticancer drug. Preclinical and clinical studies have supported the use of ECT in patients with metastatic bone disease, demonstrating that it does not damage the mineral structure of the bone and its regenerative capacity, and that is feasible and efficient for the treatment of bone metastases. Since 2009, 88 patients with bone metastasis have received ECT at the Rizzoli Institute. 2014 saw the start of a registry of patients with bone metastases treated with ECT, whose data are recorded in a shared database. We share the Rizzoli Institute experience of 38 patients treated with ECT for a bone metastasis, excluding patients not included in the registry (before 2014) and those treated with bone fixation. Mean follow-up was 2 months (1-52). Response to treatment using RECIST criteria was 29% objective responses, 59% stable disease, and 16% progressive disease. Using PERCIST, the response was 36% OR, 14% SD, and 50% PD with no significant differences between the two criteria. A significant decrease in pain and better quality of life was observed at follow up.


Clinical protocol: Patient will be anesthetized and the lytic area of bone to be treated identified. Using a Jamshidi bone needle, a core will be created allowing placement of the linear bone electrode into the lesion. Once in place, targeted electrochemotherapy will be applied into the lytic lesion. Bleomycin will be injected IV and after 8 minutes the pulse will be sent into the bone lesion allowing a transient opening of the cell membrane. 2- 3 treatments will be completed and the area wrapped upon recovery.


Follow up imaging in 4 and 8 weeks with radiographs.

", "potential_risks": "


WHAT ARE THE RISKS OF THE STUDY?


Risks to patient: 


The standard laboratory tests (blood work), ultrasound, sedation, anesthesia, and surgery carry the same risks they would if the patient were undergoing these procedures outside of the study. The TCEs under investigation have the potential to cause unwanted side effects. These unwanted side effects, anticipated to the best of our current knowledge based on studies in dogs with various tumor types, are also described below.


Blood sample collection: A small needle will be inserted into the vein of the enrolled patient to take blood samples. The total amount of blood to be obtained for study related procedures at any given visit is typically less that 5ml (roughly 1 teaspoon). Risks associated with blood draw may include some discomfort, mild irritation at the collection site, bruising, and rarely infection. Blood draws are part of standard of care for anesthesia and cancer treatment in general and may be done whether the patient participates in this study or not. The addition of intratumorally injected TCEs is not expected to alter the safety of blood sample collection. 


Tumor ultrasound: There are no known risks associated with performing ultrasound other than possible mild discomfort from pressure placed on the ultrasound probe throughout the examination. 


Surgery: The surgical protocol will be performed according to standard of care, which means that there is nothing experimental about the surgery portion of the study. There is currently no evidence to indicate that any of these standard surgical and anesthesia risks will be increased by the study drug evaluated in this study. The surgeon can discuss any standard surgery risks, including bleeding after surgery, infection at the surgery site, poor wound healing, and death.


Sedation/Anesthesia: Risks of sedation and anesthesia include low blood pressure, abnormal heart rhythms, bad reactions to the anesthesia drugs, and rarely, respiratory and/or cardiac arrest and death.


Immunotherapy Injections: The immunotherapy injections will occur through small needles, similar to those used for standard vaccines. Predictable risks associated with these TCE injections include temporary pain, minor bleeding from the injection sites, redness, and irritation at the injection site, particularly if the immune system responds to the injected agents. These TCEs are expected to affect the immune system. Therefore, temporary changes in the numbers of different immune cells within the tumor are anticipated. However, these changes are not expected to require treatment. At the veterinarian’s discretion, pain medication may be given before the tumor injections to reduce any discomfort. This is optional because the injections may not be any more painful than routine shots, blood draws, or other procedures that usually don’t require pain relief.


Human patients in clinical trials of other TCEs - given at higher doses into the bloodstream rather than directly into tumors - have sometimes experienced flu‑like symptoms, low blood pressure, and other side effects. In a prior canine clinical study testing intratumoral injection of a different TCE (not being used in this study), one patient experienced liver enzyme elevations and a systemic inflammatory response that resolved within a few days. Clinical signs included abdominal pain, two episodes of vomiting, dull mentation, increased heart rate, low blood pressure, and pale mucous membranes. Although this study seeks to reduce these risks through careful selection of the TCEs and the intratumoral doses to be used, these and other side effects, such as irritation at the injection site, release of release of chemicals in the body that can cause an overactive immune response, or injury to the intestines, hormonal system, heart, brain, lungs, and/or skin could occur. To reduce the risks of side effects in treated patients, all patients will be given oral diphenhydramine (Benadryl) 1-2 hours before injection (to help lower the risk of whole‑body allergic or anaphylactic reactions), patients will be monitored closely overnight following administration of the TCE, and the dose will be adjusted carefully between dose cohorts.


The dose and treatment schedule utilized in this study were selected to minimize risk experienced by each patient enrolled on this study. There also may be other side effects or risks that we cannot predict. Many side effects go away shortly after the drug treatment, but in some cases side effects can be serious or long-lasting or permanent.


During the course of this study, we may find out more information about the study drug, its safety, or efficacy that could be important. This information, once learned, will be made available.

  3. Tumor mass must be at least three times the volume to be injected (i.e. 900 mm3 in volume if 3x100 ml of TCE in saline or hydrogel will be injected) and must have a depth of at least 1.7 cm to accommodate needle length (1.25 cm) and minimum surgical pathology margin (0.4 cm).

", "exclusion_criteria": "

Exclusion Criteria:

  1. Weight less than 5 kg.
  2. Tumors that are anticipated by the Investigator to lack a sufficient volume of viable tumor tissue for injection due to tumor size, location, or other features based on any available pre-operative imaging (CT or ultrasound) or pathology reports describing extensive necrosis, cystic areas, or other non-viable tumor tissue.
  3. Tumors near or involving critical structures for which, in the opinion of the treating clinician, injection would pose undue risk to the patient. 
  4. Significant co-morbidities that could, in the opinion of the Investigator, interfere with adherence to the study’s procedures or requirements, or otherwise compromise the study’s objectives.
  5. History of immune-mediated disease (immune-mediated polyarthritis [IMPA], immune-mediated hemolytic anemia [IMHA], immune-mediated thrombocytopenia [ITP], myasthenia gravis, etc.) 
  6. Creatinine > 1.5x upper limit of normal (ULN)
  7. Bilirubin > 2x ULN 
  8. Hematocrit or packed cell volume < 25%
  9. Platelets < 100,000 cells/ul
  10. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) > 2.5x ULN
  11. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) ≥ 5x ULN
  12. Use of anti-coagulants ≤ 2 weeks prior to injection.
  13. Use of any nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) ≤ 3 days prior to injection.
  14. Use of JAK inhibitors (e.g., Apoquel, Zenrelia, Numelvi) ≤ 14 days prior to injection.

  18. Use of other T-cell targeting agents (CAR-T Cells, monoclonal antibodies (OX40, 4-1BB, etc.) ≤ 3 months prior to injection.

Multiple different T-cell engagers (TCE) will be delivered by injection intra-tumor with either sterile saline or hydrogel. The TCEs are engineered antibodies that bind to two targets, one on a tumor cell (B7-H3 or PD-L1) and one on a T-cell (CD3 or CD28).

WHY IS THIS STUDY BEING DONE?

Immunotherapies are a class of anti-cancer treatments that work by activating a patient’s own immune system to fight specific diseases, including cancer. A number of immunotherapies have been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in humans in a wide range of diseases, including cancer. While these therapies have shown positive results in cancers of blood cells, they have had more limited successes in solid tumors like soft tissue sarcoma. This is thought to be in part because it is hard to get enough of the drug into the tumor when it is given through the blood stream (intravenously) without causing serious side effects. To overcome this limitation, this research study will use injections of immunotherapies directly through the skin into the tumor (intra-tumoral injections). 


The primary goal of this research study is to test whether it is safe and feasible to treat tumors by injecting them with a certain type of immunotherapy called T-cell engagers (TCEs).  A T cell is a special kind of white blood cell that attacks sick cells in your body, including virus-infected cells and cancer cells. TCEs are a new kind of cancer immunotherapy that helps a patient’s own T cells find and kill cancer cells. They work like a connector: one end sticks to a cancer cell, and the other end sticks to a T cell. By pulling the two cells together, the TCE helps the T cell recognize the cancer cell and activate its killing response. In this research study, two different TCEs will be tested together (TCE combination). They work in much the same way, but each one attaches to different markers on cancer cells and T cells. Because they target different markers, the two treatments can help T cells kill cancer cells more effectively, even at lower doses of each TCE, which helps reduce the chance of harmful side effects. The goal is to make the therapy work better while still keeping patients safe.


The study will test different doses of TCEs per injection, different numbers of injections placed into the tumor itself, and the product used to dilute the TCEs. The TCE combination will be diluted either in sterile saline (a solution of salt and water) or in hydrogel (a water-based gel). The hydrogel’s job is to slowly release the drugs into the tumor, with the goal to keep the cancer cells exposed to the drugs for a longer time. This may help the treatment work better and could also reduce side effects. The TCE combination will also be mixed with sterile fluorescent dye(s) that will help researchers track where the injections were placed in the tumor. The fluorescent dye(s) have already been used in multiple canine and human clinical trials with no known side effects.  


The “investigational” part of the study are the intratumoral injections of the TCE combinations diluted in sterile saline or hydrogel. These TCEs are investigational drugs, which means they have not yet been approved by the FDA or the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for use in dogs or other species. The purpose of this study is to test the safety and the biological effect of the TCE combination in canine patients with soft tissue sarcoma (STS), rather than to specifically provide medical treatment to the enrolled patient.

L33: # Evaluation of TLR agonist Z-007 in dogs with cancer
L34: 
L35: 【11†< BACK TO ALL CLINICAL-TRIALS】
L36: 
L37:   * Recruiting
L38:   * Dog
L39:   * Oncology
L40: While significant improvements in immune based cancer treatments have been made, stimulating an effective immune response to most cancers remains a challenge. The purpose of this study is to evaluate a new agent called Z-007 that works by stimulating immune cells by binding key proteins called Toll Like Receptors (TLRs). These TLRs are responsible for alerting the immune system and helping to create inflammation, that then activates other cells that are important for killing tumor cells.
L41: Preliminary unpublished studies of Z-007 have demonstrated good activity in mouse models of cancer when Z-007 is given by either intravenous or intratumoral injection. Additionally, a previous study was completed in pet dogs with a variety of cancers to provide preliminary data on safety and effectiveness of Z-007. Of the 7 dogs treated, 3 had greater than 30% shrinkage of their tumors, and another two had unexpectedly long durations of stable disease.
L42: The Z-007 was well tolerated by all dogs, with mild nausea post treatment being the only side effect noted. In the current study, dogs with solid tumors (carcinomas, sarcomas, melanoma) will be treated with Z-007 by either intratumoral or intravenous injection, and we will follow them to determine response to treatment to identify the most effective dose and route for administration.
L43: We will also collect tumor and blood samples to understand how Z-007 alters the local and systemic immune system, with the goal of identifying key biomarkers associated with response to treatment. Together, these studies will provide important data that will help improve the use of Z-007 in dogs with cancer.
L44: ## Inclusion Criteria
L45: Pet dogs will be eligible for enrollment if they have: a solid tumor (carcinoma, sarcoma) between 2-7 cm in size that is amenable to repeat biopsy; no significant underlying co-morbidities (kidney, heart, liver disease); no abnormalities in cell or platelet counts on a complete blood count; no prior treatments with immunotherapy agents; and no history of autoimmune disease.
L46: Dogs may not have received any previous treatment for their cancer, or may have failed standard cancer treatments (surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy). While the presence of metastasis is not an exclusion factor, dogs must have a life expectancy of at least 8 weeks. Dogs must also be at least 7 kg in size.
L47: ## Exclusion Criteria
L48: 
L49:   * Significant underlying heart, kidney or liver disease
L50:   * Tumors less than 2 cm and greater than 7 cm in size will be excluded
L51: ## Client Benefits
L52: 
L53: For participation in the this clinical study, all costs associated with treatment of your dog’s cancer with Z-007 will be covered up to Day 63 of the study. The study will cover treatment for side effects related to the Z-007 administration and biopsy (i.e., vomiting, diarrhea, infection of the biopsy site) but it will not cover treatment of conditions unrelated to the study, such as bladder infection, ear infection, etc.
L54: If you choose to continue the Z-007 after Day 63, you will be responsible for the costs associated with the study visits and routine bloodwork.
L55: ## Sample or Data Requirements
L56: To be eligible for enrollment, your dog must be at least 7 kg in size, have a solid tumor (carcinoma, sarcoma, melanoma) between 2-7 cm in size that can be biopsied and/or have tumor spread (metastasis) to the lungs. Your dog must have no significant kidney, heart, or liver disease and no abnormalities on a complete blood count. Your dog must not have received any prior treatments with immune therapy, and must not have had an autoimmune disease.
L57: Your dog may have been previously treated with surgery, chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy, or may have be untreated for their cancer. Dogs may have not received any previous treatment for their cancer, or may have failed standard cancer treatments (surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy). Baseline screening tests include routine bloodwork (complete blood count, chemistry panel), a urine exam, and chest x-rays.
L58: Once enrolled in the study, your dog will have blood collected for the study (15 mls, approximately 1 tablespoon) and a tumor biopsy will be performed under sedation (this is not general anesthesia). Your dog will then have the Z-007 given by either intravenous or intratumoral injection once per week for 4 weeks (Days 0, 7, 14, 21); on Day 14, study blood will be collected again.
L59: On Day 28 of the study, the routine bloodwork and chest x-rays (if applicable) will be repeated, as well as the study blood collection and a second tumor biopsy. If your dog is doing well with either stable disease or a complete/partial shrinkage of tumor, Z-007 will be administered again on D35 and D49. The routine bloodwork, chest x-rays, study blood collection and tumor biopsy will then be repeated on D63.
L60: If your dog continues to do well, then they may recieve the Z-007 every 2 weeks for up to 6 months on a compassionate use basis. The Study Calendar on the last page of this consent provides an overview of all the required study visit and associated study activities.
